newsitem.title: USA: Police scale back search for fugitive separatist.
newsitem.headline: Police scale back search for fugitive separatist.

text.p: Police on Tuesday scaled back the search for a lone fugitive Republic of Texas militiaman who fled into the mountains as the separatist group prepared to surrender to police three days ago.

A fixed-wing airplane made a final sweep with heat-sensing equipment but bloodhounds and troopers on horseback were kept out of the rugged Davis Mountains Tuesday because of safety concerns, spokeswoman Sherri Deatherage Green said.
"The main concern is that if somebody got hurt, they might not be able to get someone in to help them," she said.
Police have opened a routine investigation into Monday's fatal shooting of a second fugitive by a handler who was leading a pack of eight hounds tracking the separatists, she said.

A brief wild-west style shootout broke out after the separatist, who police have not positively identified, fired on bloodhounds and police on the ground and in a helicopter who had tracked him to a campsite about a mile (1.6 km) from the group's compound.

Police identified the dead militia member as a "middle-aged white man," believed to be Mike Matson, 48, who was wanted for questioning. Police also were searching for Richard Keyes, 21, who was wanted on a state kidnapping charge.
Republic leader Richard McLaren, who was arrested Saturday with five members of his ragtag militia after a weeklong standoff with police, pleaded with the remaining militia member to surrender.
"Please lay down your arms. Put a white flag up or something. Lay down your arms and come in," McLaren said in a telephone interview with a Houston television station.

The man was unlikely to be able to hear McLaren's plea as he hiked on foot through one of the most remote sections of the state, a region where semi-arid grasslands stretch out before mountains peaking at up to 8,000 feet (2,438 metres) and box canyons with sheer cliff walls.

A police command post was being shut down Tuesday and all but a handful of residents allowed to return to homes they evacuated in the Davis Mountain Resort subdivision when the standoff began a week ago Sunday, Green said.
Police will continue to patrol roads around the Republic compound and the adjoining 70,000 acre U Up, U Down ranch where the lone fugitive was believed to be hiding, she said.
With his surrender Saturday, McLaren takes his fight for Texas independence into the courts where he faces federal and state charges tied to militia activity.

McLaren, 43, and his wife Evelyn McLaren, 50, were charged in a 25-count indictment with bank fraud, mail fraud and conspiracy for allegedly issuing $1.8 billion in worthless financial warrants to militia members, U.S. Attorney Paul Coggins said.
He also was being held without bond on criminal and civil contempt warrants issued earlier in Tarrant County and on state charges tied to the standoff in Jeff Davis County.

From a dilapidated trailer "embassy" in the Davis Mountain Resorts subdivision near Fort Davis, McLaren had proclaimed himself "ambassador" and sought international recognition of his claim of independence for the Republic of Texas.

The Republic of Texas group, which has now split into several factions, believed the state's 1845 annexation by the United States was illegal. Texas was an independent nation for nine years after it broke from Mexico in an 1836 rebellion.
